entries.397aced268c39eabe58ef179a0337768c5083d90: <div sID="gen1681" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Exod.13" sID="Exod.13"/> <div eID="gen1681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1682" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1683" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The commands God gave to Israel, 1. To sanctify all their firstborn to him, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.1-Exod.13.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. 2. To be sure to remember their deliverance out of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.3-Exod.13.4">v. 3, 4</reference>), and, in remembrance of it, to keep the feast of unleavened bread, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.5-Exod.13.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. 3. To transmit the knowledge of it with all possible care to their children, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.8-Exod.13.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. 4. To set apart unto God the firstlings of their cattle, (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.11-Exod.13.13">ver. 11-13</reference>), and to explain that also to their children, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.14-Exod.13.16">ver. 14-16</reference>. II. The care God took of Israel, when he had brought them out of Egypt. 1. Choosing their way for them, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.17-Exod.13.18">ver. 17, 18</reference>. 2. Guiding them in the way, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.20-Exod.13.22">ver. 20-22</reference>. And III. Their care of Joseph's bones, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.19">ver. 19</reference>.
entries.fcab441ec3b2bac76e0f7c3092a45ec86ecf6f1a: <div eID="gen1683" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1682" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sanctification of the Firstborn. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen1684" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Sanctify unto me all the firstborn, whatsoever openeth the womb among the children of Israel, <hi type="italic">both</hi> of man and of beast: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Moses said unto the people, Remember this day, in which ye came out from Egypt, out of the house of bondage; for by strength of hand the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> brought you out from this <hi type="italic">place:</hi> there shall no leavened bread be eaten. 4 This day came ye out in the month Abib. <hi type="super">5</hi> And it shall be when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall bring thee into the land of the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Amorites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites, which he sware unto thy fathers to give thee, a land flowing with milk and honey, that thou shalt keep this service in this month. <hi type="super">6</hi> Seven days thou shalt eat unleavened bread, and in the seventh day <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a feast to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">7</hi> Unleavened bread shall be eaten seven days; and there shall no leavened bread be seen with thee, neither shall there be leaven seen with thee in all thy quarters. <hi type="super">8</hi> And thou shalt show thy son in that day, saying, <hi type="italic">This is done</hi> because of that <hi type="italic">which</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> did unto me when I came forth out of Egypt. <hi type="super">9</hi> And it shall be for a sign unto thee upon thine hand, and for a memorial between thine eyes, that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's law may be in thy mouth: for with a strong hand hath the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> brought thee out of Egypt. <hi type="super">10</hi> Thou shalt therefore keep this ordinance in his season from year to year. <div eID="gen1684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1685" type="x-p"/> Care is here taken to perpetuate the remembrance, <div eID="gen1685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1686" type="x-p"/> I. Of the preservation of Israel's firstborn, when the firstborn of the Egyptians were slain. In memory of that distinguishing favour, and in gratitude for it, the firstborn, in all ages, were to be consecrated to God, as his peculiars (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.2">v. 2</reference>), and to be redeemed, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.13">v. 13</reference>. God, who by the right of creation is proprietor and sovereign of all the creatures, here lays claim in particular to the firstborn of the Israelites, by right of protection: <hi type="italic">Sanctify to me all the firstborn.</hi> The parents were not to look upon themselves as interested in their firstborn, till they had first solemnly presented them to God, recognized his title to them, and received them back, at a certain rate, from him again. Note, 1. That which is by special distinguishing mercy spared to us should be in a peculiar manner dedicated to God's honour; at least some grateful acknowledgment, in works of piety and charity, should be made, when our lives, or the lives of our children, have been given us for a prey. 2. God, who is the first and best, should have the first and best, and to him we should resign that which is most dear to us, and most valuable. The firstborn were the joy and hope of their families. Therefore <hi type="italic">they shall be mine,</hi> says God. By this it will appear that we love God best (as we ought) if we are willing to part with that to him which we love best in this world. 3. It is the <hi type="italic">church of the firstborn</hi> that is sanctified to God, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.23">Heb. xii. 23</reference>. Christ it the <hi type="italic">firstborn among many brethren</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.29">Rom. viii. 29</reference>), and, by virtue of their union with him, all that are born again, and born from above, are accounted as firstborn. There is an <hi type="italic">excellency of dignity and power</hi> belonging to them; and, <hi type="italic">if children, then heirs.</hi> <div eID="gen1686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1687" type="x-p"/> II. The remembrance of their coming out of Egypt must also be perpetuated: "<hi type="italic">Remember this day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.13.3">v. 3</reference>. Remember it by a good token, as the most remarkable day of your lives, the birthday of your nation, or the day of its coming of age, to be no longer under the rod." Thus the day of Christ's resurrection is to be remembered, for in it we were raised up with Christ out of death's <hi type="italic">house of bondage.</hi> The scripture tells us not expressly what day of the <hi type="italic">year</hi> Christ rose (as Moses told the Israelites what day of the year they were brought out of Egypt, that they might remember it yearly), but very particularly what day of the <hi type="italic">week</hi> it was, plainly intimating that, as the more valuable deliverance, and of greater importance, it should be remembered <hi type="italic">weekly.</hi> Remember it, for <hi type="italic">by strength of hand the Lord brought you out.</hi> Note, The more of God and his power appears in any deliverance, the more memorable it is. Now, that it might be remembered, <div eID="gen1687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1688" type="x-p"/> 1. They must be sure to <hi type="italic">keep the feast of unleavened bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.13.5-Exod.13.7">v. 5-7</reference>. It was not enough that they remembered it, but they must celebrate the memorial of it in that way which God had appointed, and use the instituted means of preserving the remembrance of it. So, under the gospel, we must not only remember Christ, but <hi type="italic">do this in remembrance</hi> of him. Observe, How strict the prohibition of leaven is (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.7">v. 7</reference>); not only no leaven must be eaten, but none must be seen, no, not in all their quarters. Accordingly, the Jews' usage was, before the feast of the passover, to cast all the leavened bread out of their houses: they burnt it, or buried it, or broke it small and scattered it in the wind; they searched diligently with lighted candles in all the corners of their houses, lest any leaven should remain. The care and strictness enjoined in this matter were designed, (1.) To make the feast the more solemn, and consequently the more taken notice of by their children, who would ask, "Why is so much ado made?" (2.) To teach us how solicitous we should be to put away from us all sin, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.7">1 Cor. v. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen1688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1689" type="x-p"/> 2. They must instruct their children in the meaning of it, and relate to them the story of their deliverance out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.8">v. 8</reference>. Note, (1.) Care must be taken betimes to instruct children in the knowledge of God. Here is an ancient law for catechising. (2.) It is particularly of great use to acquaint children betimes with the stories of the scripture, and to make them familiar to them. (3.) It is a debt we owe to the honour of God, and to the benefit of our children's souls, to tell them of the great works God has done for his church, both those which we have seen with our eyes done in our day and which we have heard with our ears and our fathers have told us: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt show thy son in that day</hi> (the day of the feast) these things. When they were celebrating the ordinance, they must explain it. <hi type="italic">Every thing is beautiful in its season.</hi> The passover is appointed <hi type="italic">for a sign, and for a memorial,</hi> that <hi type="italic">the Lord's law may be in thy mouth.</hi> Note, We must retain the remembrance of God's works, that we may remain under the influence of God's law. And those that have God's law in their heart should have it in their mouth, and be often speaking of it, the more to affect themselves and to instruct others.
entries.fdaefb408e551060c73320de49cf728ee3906cf5: <div eID="gen1689" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Claim upon the Firstborn. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen1690" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> And it shall be when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall bring thee into the land of the Canaanites, as he sware unto thee and to thy fathers, and shall give it thee, <hi type="super">12</hi> That thou shalt set apart unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> all that openeth the matrix, and every firstling that cometh of a beast which thou hast; the males <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's. <hi type="super">13</hi> And every firstling of an ass thou shalt redeem with a lamb; and if thou wilt not redeem it, then thou shalt break his neck: and all the firstborn of man among thy children shalt thou redeem. <hi type="super">14</hi> And it shall be when thy son asketh thee in time to come, saying, What <hi type="italic">is</hi> this? that thou shalt say unto him, By strength of hand the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> brought us out from Egypt, from the house of bondage: <hi type="super">15</hi> And it came to pass, when Pharaoh would hardly let us go, that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> slew all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both the firstborn of man, and the firstborn of beast: therefore I sacrifice to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> all that openeth the matrix, being males; but all the firstborn of my children I redeem. <hi type="super">16</hi> And it shall be for a token upon thine hand, and for frontlets between thine eyes: for by strength of hand the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> brought us forth out of Egypt. <div eID="gen1690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1691" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen1691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1692" type="x-p"/> I. Further directions concerning the dedicating of their firstborn to God. 1. The firstlings of their cattle were to be dedicated to God, as part of their possessions. Those of clean beasts—calves, lambs, and kids—if males, were to be sacrificed, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.30">Exod. xxii. 30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.18.17-Num.18.18">Num. xviii. 17, 18</reference>. Those of unclean beasts, as colts, were to be redeemed with a lamb, or knocked on the head. For whatsoever is unclean (as we all are by nature), if it be not redeemed, will be destroyed, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.11">v. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.13">13</reference>. 2. The firstborn of their children were to be redeemed, and by no means sacrificed, as the Gentiles sacrificed their children to Moloch. The price of the redemption of the firstborn was fixed by the law (<reference osisRef="Num.18.16">Num. xviii. 16</reference>) at <hi type="italic">five shekels.</hi> We were all obnoxious to the wrath and curse of God; by the blood of Christ we are redeemed, that we may be joined to the <hi type="italic">church of the firstborn.</hi> They were to redeem their children, as well as the firstlings of the unclean beasts, for our children are by nature polluted. <hi type="italic">Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?</hi> <div eID="gen1692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1693" type="x-p"/> II. Further directions concerning the catechising of their children, and all those of the rising generation, from time to time, in this matter. It is supposed that, when they saw all the firstlings thus devoted, they would ask the meaning of it, and their parents and teachers must tell them (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.14-Exod.13.16">v. 14-16</reference>) that God's special propriety in their firstborn, and all their firstlings, was founded in his special preservation of them from the sword of the destroying angel. Being thus delivered, they must serve him. Note, 1. Children should be directed and encouraged to ask their parents questions concerning the things of God, a practice which would be perhaps of all others the most profitable way of catechising; and parents must furnish themselves with useful knowledge, that they may be ready always to give an answer to their enquiries. If ever the <hi type="italic">knowledge of God cover the earth,</hi> as the waters do the sea, the fountains of family-instruction must first be broken up. 2. We should all be able to show cause for what we do in religion. As sacraments are sanctified by the word, so they must be explained and understood by it. God's service is reasonable, and it is then acceptable when we perform it intelligently, knowing what we do and why we do it. 3. It must be observed how often it is said in this chapter that <hi type="italic">by strength of hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.3">v. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.14">14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.16">16</reference>), <hi type="italic">with a strong hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.9">v. 9</reference>), the Lord brought them out of Egypt. The more opposition is given to the accomplishment of God's purposes the more is his power magnified therein. It is a strong hand that conquers hard hearts. Sometimes God is said to work deliverance <hi type="italic">not by might nor power</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.6">Zech. iv. 6</reference>), not by such visible displays of his power as that recorded here. 4. Their posterity that should be born in Canaan are directed to say, <hi type="italic">The Lord brought us out of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.13.14">v. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.16">16</reference>. Mercies to our fathers are mercies to us; we reap the benefit of them, and therefore must keep up a grateful remembrance of them. We stand upon the bottom of former deliverances, and were in the loins of our ancestors when they were delivered. Much more reason have we to say that in the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ we were redeemed.
entries.65a74923ab2702b5ecc24aaf2b8ab362811eb1f9: <div eID="gen1693" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Pillar of Fire and Fire. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen1694" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> And it came to pass, when Pharaoh had let the people go, that God led them not <hi type="italic">through</hi> the way of the land of the Philistines, although that <hi type="italic">was</hi> near; for God said, Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt: <hi type="super">18</hi> But God led the people about, <hi type="italic">through</hi> the way of the wilderness of the Red sea: and the children of Israel went up harnessed out of the land of Egypt. 19 And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him: for he had straitly sworn the children of Israel, saying, God will surely visit you; and ye shall carry up my bones away hence with you. 20 And they took their journey from Succoth, and encamped in Etham, in the edge of the wilderness. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night: <hi type="super">22</hi> He took not away the pillar of the cloud by day, nor the pillar of fire by night, <hi type="italic">from</hi> before the people. <div eID="gen1694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1695" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The choice God made of their way, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.17-Exod.13.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. He was their guide. Moses gave them direction but as he received it from the Lord. Note, The way of man is not in himself, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.23">Jer. x. 23</reference>. He may <hi type="italic">devise his way,</hi> and design it; but, after all, it is God that <hi type="italic">directs his steps,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.16.9">Prov. xvi. 9</reference>. Man proposes, but God disposes, and in his disposal we must acquiesce, and set ourselves to follow providence. There were two ways from Egypt to Canaan. One was a short cut from the north of Egypt to the south of Canaan, perhaps about four or five days' journey; the other was much further about, through the wilderness, and that was the way in which God chose to lead his people Israel, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.18">v. 18</reference>. 1. There were many reasons why God led them <hi type="italic">through the way of the wilderness of the Red Sea.</hi> The Egyptians were to be drowned in the Red Sea. The Israelites were to be humbled and proved in the wilderness, <reference osisRef="Deut.8.2">Deut. viii. 2</reference>. God had given it to Moses for a sign (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.12">ch. iii. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">You shall serve God in this mountain.</hi> They had again and again told Pharaoh that they must go <hi type="italic">three days' journey into the wilderness to do sacrifice,</hi> and therefore it was requisite that they should bend their march that way, else they would justly have been exclaimed against as notorious dissemblers. Before they entered the lists with their enemies, matters must be settled between them and their God, laws must be given, ordinances instituted, covenants sealed, and the original contract ratified, for the doing of which it was necessary that they should retire into the solitudes of a wilderness, the only closet for such a crowd; the high road would be no proper place for these transactions. It is said (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.10">Deut. xxxii. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">He led them about,</hi> some hundreds of miles about, and yet (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.7">Ps. cvii. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">He led them forth by the right way.</hi> God's way is the right way, though it seem <hi type="italic">about.</hi> If we think he leads not his people the nearest way, yet we may be sure he leads them the best way, and so it will appear when we come to our journey's end. <hi type="italic">Judge nothing before the time.</hi> 2. There was one reason why God did not lead them the nearest way, which would have brought them after a few days' march to <hi type="italic">the land of the Philistines</hi> (for it was that part of Canaan that lay next to Egypt), namely, because they were not as yet fit for war, much less for war with the Philistines, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.17">v. 17</reference>. Their spirits were broken with slavery; it was not easy for them to turn their hands of a sudden from the trowel to the sword. The Philistines were formidable enemies, too fierce to be encountered by raw recruits; it was more suitable that they should begin with the Amalekites, and be prepared for the wars of Canaan by experiencing the difficulties of the wilderness. Note, God proportions his people's trials to their strength, and will <hi type="italic">not suffer them to be tempted above what they are able,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.13">1 Cor. x. 13</reference>. That promise, if compared with the foregoing verses, will seem to refer to this event, as an instance of it. <hi type="italic">God knows our frame,</hi> and considers our weakness and faintheartedness, and by less trials will prepare us for greater. God is said to bring Israel out of Egypt as the eagle <hi type="italic">brings up her young ones</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">Deut. xxxii. 11</reference>), teaching them by degrees to fly. Orders being thus given which way they should go, we are told, (1.) That they went up themselves, not as a confused rout, but in good order, rank and file: they <hi type="italic">went up harnessed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.13.18">v. 18</reference>. They went up by <hi type="italic">five in a rank</hi> (so some), in <hi type="italic">five squadrons,</hi> so others. They marched like an army with banners, which added much to their strength and honour. (2.) That they took the <hi type="italic">bones of Joseph</hi> along with them (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.19">v. 19</reference>), and probably the bones of the rest of Jacob's sons, unless (as some think) they had been privately carried to Canaan (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.16">Acts vii. 16</reference>), severally as they died. Joseph had particularly appointed that his bones should be carried up when God should visit the (<reference osisRef="Gen.50.25-Gen.50.26">Gen. l. 25, 26</reference>), so that their carrying up his bones was not only a performance of the oath their fathers had sworn to Joseph, but an acknowledgment of the performance of God's promise to them by Joseph that he would visit them and bring them out of the land of Egypt, and an encouragement to their faith and hope that he would fulfil the other part of the promise, which was to bring them to Canaan, in expectation of which they carried these bones with them while they wandered in the desert. They might think, "Joseph's bones must rest at last, and then we shall." Moses is said to take these bones with him. Moses was now a very great man; so had Joseph been in his day, yet he was now but a box full of dry bones; this was all that remained of him in this world, which might serve for a monitor to Moses to remember his mortality. <hi type="italic">I have said, You are gods;</hi> it was said so to Moses expressly (<reference osisRef="Exod.7.1">ch. vii. 1</reference>); <hi type="italic">but you shall die like men.</hi> <div eID="gen1695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1696" type="x-p"/> II. Here is the guidance they were blessed with in the way: <hi type="italic">The Lord went before them in a pillar,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.13.21-Exod.13.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. In the first two stages it was enough that God directed Moses whither to march: he knew the country and the road well enough; but now that they had come <hi type="italic">to the edge of the wilderness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.20">v. 20</reference>) they would have occasion for a guide; and a very good guide they had, one that was infinitely wise, kind, and faithful: <hi type="italic">The Lord went before them,</hi> the <hi type="italic">shechinah</hi> (or appearance of the divine Majesty, which was typical of Christ) or a previous manifestation of the eternal Word, which, in the fulness of time, was to be <hi type="italic">made flesh,</hi> and <hi type="italic">dwell among us.</hi> Christ was with the church in the wilderness, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.9">1 Cor. x. 9</reference>. Now <hi type="italic">their King passed before them, even the Lord on the head of them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.2.13">Mic. ii. 13</reference>. Note, Those whom God brings into a wilderness he will not leave nor lose there, but will take care to lead them through it; we may well think it was a very great satisfaction to Moses and the pious Israelites to be sure that they were under divine guidance. Those needed not to fear missing their way who were thus led, nor being lost who were thus directed; those needed not to fear being benighted who were thus illuminated, nor being robbed who were thus protected. Those who make the glory of God their end, and the word of God their rule, the Spirit of God the guide of their affections, and the providence of God the guide of their affairs, may be confident that <hi type="italic">the Lord goes before them,</hi> as truly as he went before Israel in the wilderness, though not so sensibly; we must live by faith. 1. They had sensible evidences of God's going before them. They all saw an appearance from heaven of a pillar, which in the bright day appeared cloudy, and in the dark night appeared fiery. We commonly see that that which is a flame in the night is a smoke in the day; so was this. God gave them this ocular demonstration of his presence, in compassion to the infirmity of their faith, and in compliance with that infant state of the church, which needed to be thus lisped to in their own language; but blessed are <hi type="italic">those that have not seen and yet have believed</hi> God's gracious presence with them, according to his promise. 2. They had sensible effects of God's going before them in this pillar. For, (1.) It led the way in that vast howling wilderness, in which there was no road, no track, no way-mark, of which they had no maps, through which they had no guides. When they marched, this pillar went before them, at the rate that they could follow, and appointed the place of their encampment, as Infinite Wisdom saw fit, which both eased them from care, and secured them from danger, both in moving and in resting. (2.) It sheltered them by day from the heat, which, at some times of the year, was extreme. (3.) It gave them light by night when they had occasion for it, and at all times made their camp pleasant and the wilderness they were in less frightful. <div eID="gen1696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1697" type="x-p"/> III. These were constant standing miracles (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.22">v. 22</reference>): He <hi type="italic">took not away the pillar of cloud;</hi> no, not when they seemed to have less occasion for it, travelling through inhabited countries, no, not when they murmured and were provoking; it never left them, till it brought them to the borders of Canaan. It was a cloud which the wind could not scatter. This favour is acknowledged with thankfulness long afterwards, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.19">Neh. ix. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.14">Ps. lxxviii. 14</reference>. There was something spiritual in this pillar of cloud and fire. 1. The children of Israel were baptized unto Moses in this cloud, which, some think, distilled dew upon them, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.2">1 Cor. x. 2</reference>. By coming under this cloud, they signified their putting themselves under the divine guidance and command by the ministry of Moses. Protection draws allegiance; this cloud was the badge of God's protection, and so became the bond of their allegiance. Thus they were initiated, and admitted under that government, now when they were entering upon the wilderness. 2. Some make this cloud a type of Christ. The cloud of his human nature was a veil to the light and fire of his divine nature; we find him (<reference osisRef="Rev.10.1">Rev. x. 1</reference>) <hi type="italic">clothed with a cloud, and his feet as pillars of fire.</hi> Christ is our way, the light of our way and the guide of it. 3. It signified the special guidance and protection which the church of Christ is under in this world. God himself is the keeper of Israel, and he <hi type="italic">neither slumbers nor sleeps,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.121.4">Ps. cxxi. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.3">Isa. xxvii. 3</reference>. There is a defence created, not only on Sion's assemblies, but on every dwelling-place in Sion. See <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5-Isa.4.6">Isa. iv. 5, 6</reference>. Nay, every Israelite indeed is hidden under the shadow of God's wings (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">Ps. xvii. 8</reference>); angels, whose ministry was made use of in this cloud, are employed for their good, and pitch their tents about them. <hi type="italic">Happy art thou, O Israel! who is like unto thee, O people?</hi>  <chapter eID="Exod.13"/> <div eID="gen1697" type="x-p"/>

entries.c70f37a62cf9086fee408c1edfe6cebec0e1653d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv720"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <div sID="gen1015" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Exod.13.1">Ex 13:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.2">2</reference>. The First-born Sanctified.<div eID="gen1015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1016" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv720"/><hi type="bold">2. Sanctify unto me all the first-born--</hi>To "sanctify" means to "consecrate," to "set apart" from a common to a sacred use. The foundation of this duty rested on the fact that the Israelites, having had their first-born preserved by a distinguishing act of grace from the general destruction that overtook the families of the Egyptians, were bound in token of gratitude to consider them as the Lord's peculiar property (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.12.23">He 12:23</reference>). <div eID="gen1016" type="x-p"/>
entries.83f25a15c2f5b64a51457da3533b763c0e7899b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv721"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.13.3-Exod.13.10">Ex 13:3-10</reference>. Memorial of the Passover.</title> <div sID="gen1017" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv721"/><hi type="bold">3. Moses said unto the people, Remember this day--</hi>The day that gave them a national existence and introduced them into the privileges of independence and freedom, deserved to live in the memories of the Hebrews and their posterity; and, considering the signal interposition of God displayed in it, to be held not only in perpetual, but devout remembrance.<div eID="gen1017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">house of bondage--</hi>literally, "house of slaves"--that is, a servile and degrading condition.<div eID="gen1018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for by strength of hand the Lord brought you out from this place--</hi>The emancipation of Israel would never have been obtained except it had been wrung from the Egyptian tyrant by the appalling judgments of God, as had been at the outset of his mission announced to Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.19">Ex 3:19</reference>).<div eID="gen1019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">There shall no leavened bread, &c.--</hi>The words are elliptical, and the meaning of the clause may be paraphrased thus:--"For by strength of hand the Lord brought you out from this place, in such haste that there could or should be no leavened bread eaten." <div eID="gen1020" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d4e3260915ada85206e98306abfffbea6479519: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv722"/><div sID="gen1021" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv722"/><hi type="bold">4. month Abib--</hi>literally, "a green ear," and hence the month Abib is the month of green ears, corresponding to the middle of our March. It was the best season for undertaking a journey to the desert region of Sinai, especially with flocks and herds; for then the winter torrents had subsided, and the wadies were covered with an early and luxuriant verdure. <div eID="gen1021" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c95072d4c0dc00c48fcdc1311e6a6bc8c1828d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv723"/><div sID="gen1022" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv723"/><hi type="bold">5-7. when the Lord shall bring thee--</hi>The passover is here instituted as a permanent festival of the Israelites. It was, however, only a prospective observance; we read of only one celebration of the passover during the protracted sojourn in the wilderness [Nu 9:5]; but on their settlement in the promised land, the season was hallowed as a sacred anniversary [Jos 5:10], in conformity with the directions here given. <div eID="gen1022" type="x-p"/>
entries.f10b6cb55b15688bb01befdf6eb8b830ad5ecea0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv724"/><div sID="gen1023" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv724"/><hi type="bold">8. thou shalt show thy son in that day, saying--</hi>The establishment of this and the other sacred festivals presented the best opportunities of instructing the young in a knowledge of His gracious doings to their ancestors in Egypt. <div eID="gen1023" type="x-p"/>
entries.7134624763024ef1c3345a364b666268f2ba54f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv725"/><div sID="gen1024" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv725"/><hi type="bold">9. it shall be for a sign unto thee upon thine hand, &c.--</hi>There is no reason to believe that the Oriental tattooing--the custom of staining the hands with the powder of Hennah, as Eastern females now do--is here referred to. Nor is it probable that either this practice or the phylacteries of the Pharisees--parchment scrolls, which were worn on their wrists and foreheads--had so early an existence. The words are to be considered only as a figurative mode of expression.<div eID="gen1024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1025" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that the Lord's law may be in thy mouth, &c.--</hi>that is, that it may be the subject of frequent conversation and familiar knowledge among the people. <div eID="gen1025" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4017fc977fd5bdc990100e0373c556e194e06d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv726"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.13.11-Exod.13.16">Ex 13:11-16</reference>. Firstlings of Beasts.</title> <div sID="gen1026" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv726"/><hi type="bold">12-13. every firstling, &c.--</hi>the injunction respecting the consecration of the first-born, as here repeated, with some additional circumstances. The firstlings of clean beasts, such as lambs, kids, and calves, if males, were to be devoted to God and employed in sacrifice. Those unclean beasts, as the ass's colt, being unfit for sacrifice, were to be redeemed (<reference osisRef="Num.18.15">Nu 18:15</reference>). <div eID="gen1026" type="x-p"/>
entries.3780add744173e633e050b901762234681760e41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv727"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.13.17-Exod.13.21">Ex 13:17-21</reference>. Journey from Egypt.</title> <div sID="gen1027" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv727"/><hi type="bold">17. God led them not through the way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near, &c.--</hi>The shortest and most direct route from Egypt to Palestine was the usual caravan road that leads by Belbeis, El-Arish, to Ascalon and Gaza. The Philistines, who then possessed the latter, would have been sure to dispute their passage, for between them and the Israelites there was a hereditary feud (<reference osisRef="1Chr.7.21">1Ch 7:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.22">22</reference>); and so early a commencement of hostilities would have discouraged or dismayed the unwarlike band which Moses led. Their faith was to be exercised and strengthened, and from the commencement of their travels we observe the same careful proportion of burdens and trials to their character and state, as the gracious Lord shows to His people still in that spiritual journey of which the former was typical. <div eID="gen1027" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4c06b52316a4eb266fc4038aeec63d7e4c09f23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv728"/><div sID="gen1028" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv728"/><hi type="bold">18. God led the people about, through the way of the wilderness of the Red Sea, &c.--</hi>This wondrous expanse of water is a gulf of the Indian ocean. It was called in Hebrew "the weedy sea," from the forest of marine plants with which it abounds. But the name of the Red Sea is not so easily traced. Some think it was given from its contiguity to the countries of Edom ("red"); others derive it from its coral rocks; while a third class ascribe the origin of the name to an extremely red appearance of the water in some parts, caused by a numberless multitude of very small mollusca. This sea, at its northern extremity, separates into two smaller inlets--the eastern called anciently the Elanitic gulf, now the gulf of Akaba; and the western the Heroopolite gulf, now the gulf of Suez, which, there can be no doubt, extended much more to the north anciently than it does now. It was toward the latter the Israelites marched.<div eID="gen1028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1029" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went up harnessed--</hi>that is, girded, equipped for a long journey. (See <reference osisRef="Ps.105.37">Psa 105:37</reference>). The Margin renders it "five in a rank," meaning obviously five large divisions, under five presiding officers, according to the usages of all caravans; and a spectacle of such a mighty and motley multitude must have presented an imposing appearance, and its orderly progress could have been effected only by the superintending influence of God. <div eID="gen1029" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf787385900e4ea8cc0ce7e9e93ac00b5a355b54: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv729"/><div sID="gen1030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv729"/><hi type="bold">19. Moses took the bones of Joseph with him--</hi>in fulfilment of the oath he exacted from his brethren (<reference osisRef="Gen.50.25">Ge 50:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.50.26">26</reference>). The remains of the other patriarchs (not noticed from their obscurity) were also carried out of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.15">Ac 7:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.16">16</reference>); and there would be no difficulty as to the means of conveyance--a few camels bearing these precious relics would give a true picture of Oriental customs, such as is still to be seen in the immense pilgrimages to Mecca. <div eID="gen1030" type="x-p"/>
entries.2fa7fffa371ae17f52c8c6c5e5ab6bb25c885984: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv730"/><div sID="gen1031" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv730"/><hi type="bold">20. encamped in Etham--</hi>This place is supposed by the most intelligent travellers to be the modern Ajrud, where is a watering-place, and which is the third stage of the pilgrim-caravans to Mecca. "It is remarkable that either of the different routes eastward from Heliopolis, or southward from Heroopolis, equally admit of Ajrud being Etham. It is twelve miles northwest from Suez, and is literally on the edge of the desert" [Pictorial Bible]. <div eID="gen1031" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ce1e8bdc2fa55001813485685c98afb58842cae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv731"/><div sID="gen1032" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv731"/><hi type="bold">21-22. the Lord went before them--</hi>by a visible token of His presence, the Shekinah, in a majestic cloud (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.14">Psa 78:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.12">Ne 9:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.1">1Co 10:1</reference>), called "the angel of God" (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.19">Ex 14:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.20-Exod.23.23">23:20-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.99.6">Psa 99:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.99.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.8">Is 63:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">9</reference>). <chapter eID="Exod.13"/>

entries.78b22ae90acd34779628dd481a4b58595ec396fc: <div eID="gen2926" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen2927" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2928" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2928" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2927" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2929" type="x-p"/> God establishes the law concerning the first-born, and commands that all such, both of man and beast, should be sanctified unto him, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.1">Exo 13:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.2">Exo 13:2</reference>. Orders them to remember the day in which they were brought out of Egypt, when they should be brought to the land of Canaan; and to keep this service in the month Abib, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.3-Exo.13.5">Exo 13:3-5</reference>. Repeats the command concerning the leavened bread, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.6">Exo 13:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.7">Exo 13:7</reference>, and orders them to teach their children the cause of it, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.8">Exo 13:8</reference>, and to keep strictly in remembrance that it was by the might of God alone they had been delivered from Egypt, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.9">Exo 13:9</reference>. Shows that the consecration of the first-born, both of man and beast, should take place when they should be settled in Canaan, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.10-Exo.13.12">Exo 13:10-12</reference>. The first-born of man and beast to be redeemed, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.13">Exo 13:13</reference>. The reason of this also to be shown to their children, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.14">Exo 13:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.15">Exo 13:15</reference>. Frontlets or phylacteries for the hands and forehead commanded, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.16">Exo 13:16</reference>. And the people are not led directly to the promised land, but about through the wilderness; and the reason assigned, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.17">Exo 13:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.18">Exo 13:18</reference>. Moses takes the bones of Joseph with him, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.19">Exo 13:19</reference>. They journey from Succoth and come to Etham, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.20">Exo 13:20</reference>. And the Lord goes before them by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.21">Exo 13:21</reference>, which miracle is regularly continued both by day and night, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.22">Exo 13:22</reference>. <div eID="gen2929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2930" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen2930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2931" type="x-p"/> The Lord spake unto Moses - The commands in this chapter appear to have been given at Succoth, on the same day in which they left Egypt.
entries.1b31a44662149502f00c40dfe7ca6f11fcbfe3cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen2931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2932" type="x-p"/> Sanctify unto me all the first-born - To sanctify, קדש kadash, signifies to consecrate, separate, and set apart a thing or person from all secular purposes to some religious use; and exactly answers to the import of the Greek ἁγιαζω, from a, privative, and γη, the earth, because every thing offered or consecrated to God was separated from all earthly uses. Hence a holy person or saint is termed ἁγιος, i.e., a person separated from the earth; one who lives a holy life, entirely devoted to the service of God. Thus the persons and animals sanctified to God were employed in the service of the tabernacle and temple; and the animals, such as were proper, were offered in sacrifice. <div eID="gen2932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2933" type="x-p"/> The Hindoos frequently make a vow, and devote to an idol the first-born of a goat and of a man. The goat is permitted to run wild, as a consecrated animal. A child thus devoted has a lock of hair separated, which at the time appointed is cut off and placed near the idol. Hindoo women sometimes pray to Gunga (the Ganges) for children, and promise to devote the first-born to her. Children thus devoted are cast into the Ganges, but are generally saved by the friendly hand of some stranger - Ward's Customs. <div eID="gen2933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2934" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever openeth the womb - That is, the first-born, if a male; for females were not offered, nor the first male, if a female had been born previously. Again, if a man had several wives, the first-born of each, if a male, was to be offered to God. And all this was done to commemorate the preservation of the first-born of the Israelites, when those of the Egyptians were destroyed.
entries.edfe04d2806cf5bc232e4c90a63e7bb228515d5b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen2934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2935" type="x-p"/> When the Lord shall bring thee into the land - Hence it is pretty evident that the Israelites were not obliged to celebrate the Passover, or keep the feast of unleavened bread, till they were brought into the promised land.
entries.c742103884514bb3e707a104b713e8b43010f6a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen2935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2936" type="x-p"/> Unleavened bread - See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Exo.12.15">Exo 12:15</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Exo.12.16">Exo 12:16</reference> (note).
entries.81ec799218ed42093c8583443ef12cf72e7c56ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen2936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2937" type="x-p"/> And it shall be for a sign - upon thine hand - This direction, repeated and enlarged <reference osisRef="Exo.13.16">Exo 13:16</reference>, gave rise to phylacteries or tephillin, and this is one of the passages which the Jews write upon them to the present day. The manner in which the Jews understood and kept these commands may appear in their practice. They wrote the following four portions of the law upon slips of parchment or vellum: Sanctify unto me the first-born, Exodus 13, from <reference osisRef="Exo.13.2-Exo.13.10">Exo 13:2-10</reference> inclusive. And it shall be, when the Lord shall bring thee into the land, Exodus 13, from <reference osisRef="Exo.13.11-Exo.13.16">Exo 13:11-16</reference> inclusive. Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord, Deuteronomy 6, from <reference osisRef="Deu.6.4-Deu.6.9">Deu 6:4-9</reference> inclusive. And it shall come to pass, if ye shall hearken diligently, Deuteronomy 11, from <reference osisRef="Deu.11.13-Deu.11.21">Deu 11:13-21</reference> inclusive. These four portions, making in all 30 verses, written as mentioned above, and covered with leather, they tied to the forehead and to the hand or arm. <div eID="gen2937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2938" type="x-p"/> Those which were for the Head (the frontlets) they wrote on four slips of parchment, and rolled up each by itself, and placed them in four compartments, joined together in one piece of skin or leather. Those which were designed for the hand were formed of one piece of parchment, the four portions being written upon it in four columns, and rolled up from one end to the other. These were all correct transcripts from the Mosaic text, without one redundant or deficient letter, otherwise they were not lawful to be worn. Those for the head were tied on so as to rest on the forehead. Those for the hand or arm were usually tied on the left arm, a little above the elbow, on the inside, that they might be near the heart, according to the command, <reference osisRef="Deu.6.6">Deu 6:6</reference> : And these words which I command thee this day shall be in thine heart. These phylacteries formed no inconsiderable part of a Jew's religion; they wore them as a sign of their obligation to God, and as representing some future blessedness. Hence they did not wear them on feast days nor on the Sabbath, because these things were in themselves signs; but they wore them always when they read the law, or when they prayed, and hence they called them תפלין tephillin, prayer, ornaments, oratories, or incitements to prayer. In process of time the spirit of this law was lost in the letter, and when the word was not in their mouth, nor the law in their heart, they had their phylacteries on their heads and on their hands. And the Pharisees, who in our Lord's time affected extraordinary piety, made their phylacteries very broad, that they might have many sentences written upon them, or the ordinary portions in very large and observable letters. <div eID="gen2938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2939" type="x-p"/> It appears that the Jews wore these for three different purposes: - <div eID="gen2939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2940" type="x-p"/> 1. As signs or remembrancers. This was the original design, as the institution itself sufficiently proves. <div eID="gen2940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2941" type="x-p"/> 2. To procure reverence and respect in the sight of the heathen. This reason is given in the Gemara, Berachoth, chapter i: "Whence is it proved that the phylacteries or tephillin are the strength of Israel? Ans. From what is written, <reference osisRef="Deu.28.10">Deu 28:10</reference> : All the people of the earth shall see that thou art called by the name of the Lord (יהוה Yehovah) and they shall be afraid of thee." <div eID="gen2941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2942" type="x-p"/> 3. They used them as amulets or charms, to drive away evil spirits. This appears from the Targum on <reference osisRef="Sol.8.3">Sol 8:3</reference> : His left hand is under my head, etc. "The congregation of Israel hath said, I am elect above all people, because I bind my phylacteries on my left hand and on my head, and the scroll is fixed to the right side of my gate, the third part of which looks to my bed-chamber, that demons may not be permitted to injure me. <div eID="gen2942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2943" type="x-p"/> One of the original phylacteries or תפלין tephillin now lies before me; it is a piece of fine vellum, about eighteen inches long, and an inch and quarter broad. It is divided into four unequal compartments; the letters are very well formed, but written with many apices, after the manner of the German Jews. In the first compartment is written the portion taken from <reference osisRef="Exo.13.2-Exo.13.10">Exo 13:2-10</reference>; in the second, <reference osisRef="Exo.13.11-Exo.13.16">Exo 13:11-16</reference>; in the third, <reference osisRef="Deu.6.4-Deu.6.9">Deu 6:4-9</reference>; in the fourth, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.13-Deu.11.21">Deu 11:13-21</reference>, as before related. This had originally served for the hand or arm. <div eID="gen2943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2944" type="x-p"/> These passages seem to be chosen in vindication of the use of the phylactery itself, as the reader may see on consulting them at large. Bind them for a Sign upon thy Hand; and for Frontlets between thy Eyes; write them upon the Posts of thy House and upon thy Gates; all which commands the Jews take in the most literal sense. To acquire the reputation of extraordinary sanctity they wore the fringes of their garments of an uncommon length. Moses had commanded them, <reference osisRef="Num.15.38">Num 15:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.15.39">Num 15:39</reference>, to put fringes to the borders of their garments, that when they looked upon even these distinct threads they might remember, not only the law in general but also the very minutiae or smaller parts of all the precepts, rites, and ceremonies belonging to it. As those hypocrites (for such our Lord proves them to be) were destitute of all the life and power of religion within, they endeavored to supply its place with phylacteries and fringes without. The same principles distinguish hypocrites every where, and multitudes of them may be found among those termed Christians as well as among the Jews. It is probably to this institution relative to the phylactery that the words, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.1">Rev 14:1</reference>, allude: And I looked, and, lo, a hundred and forty-four thousand having his Father's name written on their foreheads. "That is," says Mr. Ainsworth, "as a sign of the profession of God's law; for That which in the Gospel is called his Name, (<reference osisRef="Mat.12.21">Mat 12:21</reference>), in the prophets is called his Law, (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.4">Isa 42:4</reference>)." So again antichrist exacts the obedience to his precepts by a mark on men's right hands or on their foreheads, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.16">Rev 13:16</reference>.
entries.c16602156cb60484c098ffe56c608138b2db7d62: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen2944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2945" type="x-p"/> Every firstling of an ass thou shalt redeem with a lamb - Or a kid, as in the margin. In <reference osisRef="Num.18.15">Num 18:15</reference>, it is said: "The first-born of man shalt thou surely redeem; and the firstling of an unclean beast shalt thou redeem." Hence we may infer that ass is put here for any unclean beast, or for unclean beasts in general. The lamb was to be given to the Lord, that is, to his priest, <reference osisRef="Num.18.8">Num 18:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.18.15">Num 18:15</reference>. And then the owner of the ass might use it for his own service, which without this redemption he could not do; see <reference osisRef="Deu.15.19">Deu 15:19</reference>. <div eID="gen2945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2946" type="x-p"/> The first-born of man - shalt thou redeem - This was done by giving to the priests five standard shekels, or shekels of the sanctuary, every shekel weighing twenty gerahs. What the gerah was, see Clarke on <reference osisRef="Gen.20.16">Gen 20:16</reference> (note). And for the shekel, see Clarke on <reference osisRef="Gen.20.16">Gen 20:16</reference> (note). <div eID="gen2946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2947" type="x-p"/> It may be necessary to observe here that the Hebrew doctors teach, that if a father had neglected or refused thus to redeem his first-born, the son himself was obliged to do it when he came of age. As this redeeming of the first-born was instituted in consequence of sparing the first-born of the Israelites, when the first-born both of man and beast among the Egyptians was destroyed, on this ground all the first-born were the Lord's, and should have been employed in his service; but he permitted the first-born of a useful unclean animal to be redeemed by a clean animal of much less value. And he chose the tribe of Levi in place of all the first-born of the tribes in general; and the five shekels were ordered to be paid in lieu of such first-born sons as were liable to serve in the sanctuary, and the money was applied to the support of the priests and Levites. See this subject at large in <reference osisRef="Num.3.12">Num 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.3.13">Num 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.3.41">Num 3:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.3.43">Num 3:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.3.45">Num 3:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.3.47-Num.3.51">Num 3:47-51</reference>.
entries.20f298e7df2cd9af76b86d9a89968925ecc0c236: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen2947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2948" type="x-p"/> It shall be for a token, etc. - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.13.9">Exo 13:9</reference>.
entries.c5f394e9eecdb91efb3bf08a362cc7569887fdd9: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen2948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2949" type="x-p"/> God led them not through the way of the land of the Philistines, etc. - Had the Israelites been obliged to commence their journey to the promised land by a military campaign, there is little room to doubt that they would have been discouraged, have rebelled against Moses and Aaron, and have returned back to Egypt. Their long slavery had so degraded their minds that they were incapable of any great or noble exertions; and it is only on the ground of this mental degradation, the infallible consequence of slavery, that we can account for their many dastardly acts, murmurings, and repinings after their escape from Egypt. The reader is requested to bear this in mind, as it will serve to elucidate several circumstances in the ensuing history. Besides, the Israelites were in all probability unarmed, and totally unequipped for battle, encumbered with their flocks, and certain culinary utensils. which they were obliged to carry with them in the wilderness to provide them with bread, etc.
entries.6e7158b8610831fe233868abf38df69af1d31f93: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen2949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2950" type="x-p"/> But God led the people about - Dr. Shaw has shown that there were two roads from Egypt to Canaan, one through the valleys of Jendilly, Rumeleah, and Baideah, bounded on each side by the mountains of the lower Thebais; the other lies higher, having the northern range of the mountains of Mocatee running parallel with it on the right hand, and the desert of the Egyptian Arabia, which lies all the way open to the land of the Philistines, to the left. See his account of these encampments at the end of Exodus. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.40.38">Exo 40:38</reference>. <div eID="gen2950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2951" type="x-p"/> Went up harnessed - חמשים chamushim. It is truly astonishing what a great variety of opinions are entertained relative to the meaning of this word. After having maturely considered all that I have met with on the subject, I think it probable that the word refers simply to that orderly or well arranged manner in which the Israelites commenced their journey from Egypt. For to arrange, array, or set in order, seems to be the ideal meaning of the word חמש chamash. As it was natural to expect that in such circumstances there must have been much hurry and confusion, the inspired writer particularly marks the contrary, to show that God had so disposed matters that the utmost regularity and order prevailed; and had it been otherwise, thousands of men, women, and children must have been trodden to death. Our margin has it by five in a rank; but had they marched only five abreast, supposing only one yard for each rank to move in, it would have required not less than sixty-eight miles for even the 600,000 to proceed on regularly in this way; for 600,000 divided by five gives 120,000 ranks of five each; and there being only 1,760 yards in a mile, the dividing 120,000 by 1,760 will give the number of miles such a column of people would take up, which by such an operation will be found to be something more than sixty-eight miles. But this the circumstances of the history will by no means admit - Harmer. The simple meaning therefore appears to be that given above; and if the note on the concluding verse of the preceding chapter be considered, it may serve to place this explanation in a still clearer point of view.
entries.ff8fcfb5685fcca8c05f38e2fd179a0554fa0ba6: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen2951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2952" type="x-p"/> Moses took the bones of Joseph - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.50.25">Gen 50:25</reference>. It is supposed that the Israelites carried with them the bones or remains of all the twelve sons of Jacob, each tribe taking care of the bones of its own patriarch, while Moses took care of the bones of Joseph. St. Stephen expressly says, <reference osisRef="Act.7.15">Act 7:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.7.16">Act 7:16</reference>, that not only Jacob, but the fathers were carried from Egypt into Sychem; and this, as Calmet remarks, was the only opportunity that seems to have presented itself for doing this: and certainly the reason that rendered it proper to remove the bones of Joseph to the promised land, had equal weight in reference to those of the other patriarchs. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.49.29">Gen 49:29</reference>.
entries.3801010f5596455bd22987b0f4a7c2fb4ee0553b: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen2952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2953" type="x-p"/> Encamped in Etham - As for the reasons assigned on <reference osisRef="Exo.13.17">Exo 13:17</reference>, God would not lead the Israelites by the way of the Philistines' country, he directed them towards the wilderness of Shur, <reference osisRef="Exo.15.22">Exo 15:22</reference>, upon the edge or extremity of which, next to Egypt, at the bottom of the Arabian Gulf, lay Etham, which is the second place of encampment mentioned. See the extracts from Dr. Shaw at the end of Exodus. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.40.38">Exo 40:38</reference>.
entries.db458ddde92125c93a1906ba5ab315fccb082760: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen2953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2954" type="x-p"/> The Lord went before them - That by the Lord here is meant the Lord Jesus, we have the authority of St. Paul to believe, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.9">1Cor 10:9</reference> : it was he whose Spirit they tempted in the wilderness, for it was he who led them through the desert to the promised rest. <div eID="gen2954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2955" type="x-p"/> Pillar of a cloud - This pillar or column, which appeared as a cloud by day, and a fire by night, was the symbol of the Divine presence. This was the Shechinah or Divine dwelling place, and was the continual proof of the presence and protection of God. It was necessary that they should have a guide to direct them through the wilderness, even had they taken the most direct road; and how much more so when they took a circuitous route not usually traveled, and of which they knew nothing but just as the luminous pillar pointed out the way! Besides, it is very likely that even Moses himself did not know the route which God had determined on, nor the places of encampment, till the pillar that went before them became stationary, and thus pointed out, not only the road, but the different places of rest. Whether there was more than one pillar is not clearly determined by the text. If there was but one it certainly assumed three different appearances, for the performance of Three very important offices. 1. In the day-time, for the purpose of pointing out the way, a column or pillar of a cloud was all that was requisite. 2. At night, to prevent that confusion which must otherwise have taken place, the pillar of cloud became a pillar of fire, not to direct their journeyings, for they seldom traveled by night, but to give light to every part of the Israelitish camp. 3. In such a scorching, barren, thirsty desert, something farther was necessary than a light and a guide. Women, children, and comparatively infirm persons, exposed to the rays of such a burning sun, must have been destroyed if without a covering; hence we find that a cloud overshadowed them: and from what St. Paul observes, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.1">1Cor 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.2">1Cor 10:2</reference>, we are led to conclude that this covering cloud was composed of aqueous particles for the cooling of the atmosphere and refreshment of themselves and their cattle; for he represents the whole camp as being sprinkled or immersed in the humidity of its vapours, and expressly calls it a being under the cloud and being baptized in the cloud. To the circumstance of the cloud covering them, there are several references in Scripture. Thus: He spread a Cloud for their Covering; <reference osisRef="Psa.105.39">Psa 105:39</reference>. And the Lord will create upon every dwelling place of Mount Zion, and upon her assemblies, A Cloud and Smoke By Day, and the shining of a Flaming Fire by night; for upon all the glory shall be a Defence, (or Covering), <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Isa 4:5</reference>; which words contain the most manifest allusion to the threefold office of the cloud in the wilderness. See <reference osisRef="Num.9.16-Num.9.18">Num 9:16-18</reference>, etc.
entries.f19eb23c59f0400b7c22d091db8e29b1a5588815: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen2955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2956" type="x-p"/> He took not away the pillar of the cloud - Neither Jews nor Gentiles are agreed how long the cloud continued with the Israelites. It is very probable that it first visited them at Succoth, if it did not accompany them from Rameses; and that it continued with them till they came to the river Jordan, to pass over opposite to Jericho, for after that it appears that the ark alone was their guide, as it always marched at their head. See <reference osisRef="Jos.3.10-Jos.3.11">Jos 3:10-11</reference>, etc. But others think that it went no farther with them than Mount Hor, and never appeared after the death of Aaron. We may safely assert that while it was indispensably necessary it continued with them, when it was not so it was removed. But it is worthy of remark that the ark of the covenant became its substitute. While a miracle was necessary, a miracle was granted; when that was no longer necessary, then the testimony of the Lord deposited in the ark was deemed sufficient by Him who cannot err. So, under the Gospel dispensation, miracles were necessary at its first promulgation; but after that the canon of Scripture was completed, the new covenant having been made, ratified by the blood of the Lamb, and published by the Holy Spirit, then God withdrew generally those outward signs, leaving his word for a continual testimony, and sealing it on the souls of believers by the Spirit of truth. <div eID="gen2956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2957" type="x-p"/> It is also worthy of remark that the ancient heathen writers represent their gods, in their pretended manifestations to men, as always encompassed with a cloud; Homer and Virgil abound with examples of this kind: and is it not very probable that they borrowed this, as they did many other things in their mythologic theology, from the tradition of Jehovah guiding his people through the desert by means of the cloud, in and by which he repeatedly manifested himself? <div eID="gen2957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2958" type="x-p"/> 1. Extraordinary manifestations and interpositions of providence and grace should be held in continual remembrance. We are liable to forget the hole of the pit whence we were dug, and the rock whence we were hewn. Prudence and piety will institute their anniversaries, that the merciful dealings of the Lord may never be forgotten. The passover and the feast of unleavened bread, by an annual commemoration, became standing proofs to the children of Israel of the Divine origin of their religion; and are supporting pillars of it to the present day. For when a fact is reported to have taken place, and certain rites or ceremonies have been instituted in order to commemorate it, which rites or ceremonies continue to be observed through succeeding ages, then the fact itself, no matter how remote the period of its occurrence may have been, has the utmost proofs of authenticity that it is possible for any fact to have; and such as every person pretending to reason and judgment is obliged to receive. On this ground the Mosaic religion, and the facts recorded in it, are indubitably proved; and the Christian religion and its facts, being commemorated in the same way, particularly by baptism and the Lord's Supper, stand on such a foundation of moral certainty as no other records in the universe can possibly boast. Reader, praise God for his ordinances; they are not only means of grace to thy soul, but standing irrefragable proofs of the truth of that religion which thou hast received as from Him. <div eID="gen2958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2959" type="x-p"/> 2. A serious public profession of the religion of Christ has in all ages of the Church been considered not only highly becoming, but indispensably necessary to salvation. He who consistently confesses Christ before men shall be confessed by him before God and his angels. A Jew wore his phylacteries on his forehead, on his hands, and round his garments, that he might have reverence in the sight of the heathen; he gloried in his law, and he exulted that Abraham was his father. Christian! with a zeal not less becoming, and more consistently supported, let the words of thy mouth, the acts of thy hands, and all thy goings, show that thou belongest unto God; that thou hast taken his Spirit for the guide of thy heart, his word for the rule of thy life, his people for thy companions, his heaven for thy inheritance, and himself for the portion of thy soul. And see that thou hold fast the truth, and that thou hold it in righteousness. <div eID="gen2959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2960" type="x-p"/> 3. How merciful is God in the dispensations of his providence! He permits none to be tried above what he is able to bear, and he proportions the burden to the back that is to bear it. He led not the Israelites by the way of the Philistines, lest, seeing war, they should repent and be discouraged. Young converts are generally saved from severe spiritual conflicts and heavy temptations till they have acquired a habit of believing, are disciplined in the school of Christ, and instructed in the nature of the path in which they go, and the difficulties they may expect to find in it. They are informed that such things may take place, they are thus armed for the battle, and when trials do come they are not taken by surprise. God, the most merciful and kind God, "tempers even the blast to the shorn lamb." Trust in him therefore with all thy heart, and never lean to thy own understanding. <div eID="gen2960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2961" type="x-p"/> 4. The providence and goodness of God are equally observable in the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire. The former was the proof of his providential kindness by day; the latter, by night. Thus he adjusts the assistance of his grace and Spirit to the exigencies of his creatures, giving at some times, when peculiar trials require it, more particular manifestations of his mercy and goodness; but at all times, such evidences of his approbation as are sufficient to satisfy a pious faithful heart. It is true the pillar of fire was more observable in the night, because of the general darkness, than the pillar of cloud was by day; yet the latter was as convincing and as evident a proof of his presence, approbation, and protection as the former. It is the duty and interest of every sound believer in Christ to have the witness of God's Spirit in his soul at all times, that his spirit and ways please his Maker; but in seasons of peculiar difficulty he may expect the more sensible manifestations of God's goodness. A good man is a temple of the Holy Spirit; but he who has an unholy heart, and who lives an unrighteous life, though he may have an orthodox creed, is a hold of unclean spirits, and an abomination in the sight of the Lord. Reader, let not these observations be fruitless to thee. God gives thee his word and his Spirit, obey this word that thou grieve not this Spirit. The following figurative saying of a Jewish rabbin is worthy of regard: "God addresses Israel and says, My son, I give thee my lamp, give me thy lamp. If thou keep my lamp, I will keep thy lamp; but if thou quench my lamp, I will extinguish thy lamp:" i.e., I give thee my word and Spirit, give me thy heart and soul. If thou carefully attend to my word, and grieve not my Spirit. I will preserve thy soul alive; but if thou rebel against my word, and quench my Spirit, then thy light shall be put out, and thy soul's blessedness extinguished in everlasting darkness.  <chapter eID="Exod.13"/> <div eID="gen2961" type="x-p"/>

entries.a44061a806a07a88935ef88bb29048a270829349: Sanctification of the first-born, and Promulgation of the Law for the Feast of Mazzoth. - <reference osisRef="Exod.13.1">Exo 13:1</reference>, Exo 13:2. The sanctification of the first-born was closely connected with the Passover. By this the deliverance of the Israelitish first-born was effected, and the object of this deliverance was their sanctification. Because Jehovah had delivered the first-born of Israel, they were to be sanctified to Him. If the Israelites completed their communion with Jehovah in the Passover, and celebrated the commencement of their divine standing in the feast of unleavened bread, they gave uninterrupted effect to their divine sonship in the sanctification of the first-born. For this reason, probably, the sanctification of the first-born was commanded by Jehovah at Succoth, immediately after the Exodus, and contemporaneously with the institution of the seven days’ feast of Mazzoth (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.2.15">Exo 2:15</reference>), so that the place assigned it in the historical record is the correct one; whereas the divine appointment of the feast of Mazzoth had been mentioned before (Exo 12:15.), and the communication of that appointment to the people was all that remained to be mentioned here.
entries.f6676cc03d3c6329d534cb79707100142a7e3ed2: <reference osisRef="Exod.13.2">Exo 13:2</reference> <div eID="gen784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen785" type="x-p"/> Every first-born of man and beast was to be sanctified to <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, i.e., given up to Him for His service. As the expression, “all the first-born,” applied to both man and beast, the explanation is added, “<hi type="italic">everything that opens the womb among the Israelites, of man and beast</hi>.” כּל־רחם פּטר for רחם כּל־פּטת (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.12">Exo 13:12</reference>): כּל is placed like an adjective after the noun, as in Num 8:16, כּל בּכור for בּכור־כּל, διανοῖγον πᾶσαν μήτραν for πᾶν διανοῖγον μήτραν (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.12">Exo 13:12</reference>, lxx). הוּא לי: “<hi type="italic">it is Mine,</hi>” it belongs to Me. This right to the first-born was not founded upon the fact, that “Jehovah was the Lord and Creator of all things, and as every created object owed its life to Him, to Him should its life be entirely devoted,” as <hi type="italic">Kurtz</hi> maintains, though without scriptural proof; but in Num 3:13 and Num 8:17 the ground of the claim is expressly mentioned, viz., that on the day when <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> smote all the first-born of Egypt, He sanctified to Himself all the first-born of the Israelites, both of man and beast. Hence the sanctification of the first-born rested not upon the deliverance of the first-born sons from the stroke of the destroyer through the atoning blood of the paschal lamb, but upon the fact that God sanctified them for Himself at that time, and therefore delivered them. But Jehovah sanctified the first-born of Israel to Himself by adopting Israel as His first-born son (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.22">Exo 4:22</reference>), or as His possession. Because Israel had been chosen as the nation of Jehovah, its first-born of man and beast were spared, and for that reason they were henceforth to be sanctified to Jehovah. In what way, is more clearly defined in Num 8:12.
entries.697c96115d16b7aabfaca0200a983deb142c0b73: <reference osisRef="Exod.13.3-Exod.13.7">Exo 13:3-7</reference> <div eID="gen785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen786" type="x-p"/> The directions as to the seven days’ feast of unleavened bread (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.15-Exod.12.20">Exo 12:15-20</reference>) were made known by Moses to the people on the day of the Exodus, at the first station, namely, Succoth; but in the account of this, only the most important points are repeated, and the yearly commemoration is enjoined. In <reference osisRef="Exod.13.3">Exo 13:3</reference>, Egypt is called a “<hi type="italic">slave-house,</hi>” inasmuch as Israel was employed in slave-labour there, and treated as a slave population (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.20.2">Exo 20:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.5.6">Deu 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.6.12">Deu 6:12</reference>, etc.). יד הזק “<hi type="italic">strength of hand,</hi>” in <reference osisRef="Exod.13.3">Exo 13:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.14">Exo 13:14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Exod.13.16">Exo 13:16</reference>, is more emphatic than the more usual חזקה יד (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.19">Exo 3:19</reference>, etc.). - On <reference osisRef="Exod.13.5">Exo 13:5</reference>, see <reference osisRef="Exod.3.8">Exo 3:8</reference>, and Exo 12:25. In <reference osisRef="Exod.13.6">Exo 13:6</reference>, the term “<hi type="italic">feast to Jehovah</hi>” points to the keeping of the seventh day by a holy convocation and the suspension of work (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.16">Exo 12:16</reference>). It is only of the seventh day that this is expressly stated, because it was understood as a matter of course, that the first was a feast of <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>.
entries.435a8db21cdd41fc59bd8b373ce211e225b160fa: <reference osisRef="Exod.13.8">Exo 13:8</reference> <div eID="gen786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen787" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">because of that which Jehovah did to me</hi>” (זה in a relative sense, <hi type="italic">is qui</hi>, for אשׁר, see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §331): sc., “I eat unleavened bread,” or, “I observe this service.” This completion of the imperfect sentence follows readily from the context, and the whole verse may be explained from <reference osisRef="Exod.12.26">Exo 12:26</reference>-27.
entries.c3f8c1e607b3623d2cb64e273ce8aedfe354c86c: <reference osisRef="Exod.13.9">Exo 13:9</reference> <div eID="gen787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen788" type="x-p"/> The festival prescribed was to be to Israel “<hi type="italic">for a sign upon its hand, and for a memorial between the eyes</hi>.” These words presuppose the custom of wearing mnemonic signs upon the hand and forehead; but they are not to be traced to the heathen custom of branding soldiers and slaves with marks upon the hand and forehead. For the parallel passages in <reference osisRef="Deut.6.8">Deu 6:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.11.18">Deu 11:18</reference>, “bind them for a sign upon your hand,” are proofs that the allusion is neither to branding nor writing on the hand. Hence the sign upon the hand probably consisted of a bracelet round the wrist, and the <hi type="italic">ziccaron</hi> between the eyes, of a band worn upon the forehead. The words are then used figuratively, as a proverbial expression employed to give emphasis to the injunction to bear this precept continually in mind, to be always mindful to observe it. This is still more apparent from the reason assigned, “<hi type="italic">that the law of Jehovah may be in thy mouth</hi>.” For it was not by mnemonic slips upon the hand and forehead that a law was so placed in the mouth as to be talked of continually (<reference osisRef="Deut.6.7">Deu 6:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.19">Deu 11:19</reference>), but by the reception of it into the heart and its continual fulfilment. (See also Exo 13:16.) As the origin and meaning of the festival were to be talked of in connection with the eating of unleavened bread, so conversation about the law of Jehovah was introduced at the same time, and the obligation to keep it renewed and brought vividly to mind.
entries.7c06f609929d2fd8c8848d0d3234533547f9d428: <reference osisRef="Exod.13.10">Exo 13:10</reference> <div eID="gen788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen789" type="x-p"/> This ordinance the Israelites were to keep למועדהּ, “<hi type="italic">at its appointed time</hi>” (i.e., from the 15th to the 21st Abib), - “<hi type="italic">from days to days,</hi>” i.e., as often as the days returned, therefore from year to year (cf. Jdg 11:40; Jdg 21:19; <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.3">1Sa 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.19">1Sa 2:19</reference>).
